Surah al-Anfal is Madani, and its verses number seventy-five.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿They ask you about the spoils of war.﴾ That is, about the ghanaim (spoils), meaning their ruling. The spoils were called nafl (ʾanfāl, sing. nafl) because they are a gift and bounty from Allah, just as the term is applied to what the leader stipulates for one who ventures into a perilous undertaking, as a gift to him and an addition over his share.

﴿Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger.﴾ That is, their disposition is exclusively theirs; the Messenger distributes them as Allah commands him.

The occasion of revelation was the disagreement of the Muslims over the spoils of Badr: how they were to be divided, and who was to divide them, the Emigrants (Muhajirun) among them or the Helpers (Ansar). It was also said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had stipulated that whoever had shown valour (ghana) would receive a nafl, so their young men hastened forward, and they killed seventy and captured seventy, and then demanded their nafl. The wealth was small. The elders and notables who had been beside the banners said: "We were a reserve for you and a company to whom you could retreat." So it was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divided it among them equally. From this it has been said that the leader is not obliged to fulfil what he has promised; this is the view of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him. And on the authority of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "On the day of Badr, my brother ʿUmayr was killed, so I killed Saʿid ibn al-ʿAs in retaliation for him and took his sword. I brought it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and asked him to grant it to me. He said: 'This is neither for me nor for you; throw it into the spoils.' So I threw it there, and I had within me what none knows but Allah, of the killing of my brother and the taking of my spoils. I had not gone far before Surah al-Anfal was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: 'You asked me for the sword when it was not mine, and now it has become mine, so go and take it.'"

It is read "yasʾalūnaka al-anfāl," with the hamza elided and the fa'l vowel transferred to the lam, and the nun of ʿan assimilated into it; and "yasʾalūnaka al-anfāl" means that the young men are asking you for what you stipulated for them. ﴿So fear Allah﴾ in the disagreement and dispute.

﴿And set right the state of affairs among yourselves﴾: the condition between you, by mutual consolation and assistance in what Allah has provided you, and by surrendering the matter to Allah and His Messenger.

﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ in this. ﴿If you are believers﴾: for faith requires that; or, if you are those of perfect faith, for the perfection of faith rests on these three: obedience to the commands, abstaining from sins, and setting right the state of affairs among people with justice and excellence.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 2–4:

﴿Truly, the believers﴾ i.e., those who are perfect in faith. ﴿are those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned﴾ they are startled at His remembrance, out of magnifying Him and standing in awe of His majesty. It is also said that this refers to the man who intends to commit a sin, and when he is told, "Fear God," he refrains from it out of fear of His punishment. It was also read as "wajalat" with a fatha (وَجَلَتْ), which is a dialect form, and "faraqat" means "feared." ﴿And when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾ either because of the increase in the believer's belief in Him, or because of the tranquility of the soul and the firmness of certainty through the convergence of proofs, or through acting upon what they require. This is the view of those who say that faith increases through obedience and decreases through disobedience, on the basis that action is included within it. ﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾ they entrust their affairs to Him, and they fear none but Him and hope in none but Him.

(p-50) ﴿Those who establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them﴾.

﴿Those are the true believers﴾ because they have realized their faith by adding to it the noble deeds of the heart, namely fear (khashyah), sincerity (ikhlas), and reliance (tawakkul), and the excellent acts of the limbs, which are the measure of these, namely prayer and charity. ﴿Truly﴾ is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), or an emphatic verbal noun, like the saying: "He is the servant of God, truly (haqqan)." ﴿For them are ranks with their Lord﴾ honor and elevation of station.

It is also said: the ranks of Paradise, which they ascend by their deeds. ﴿And forgiveness﴾ for what has passed from them. ﴿And a generous provision﴾ prepared for them in Paradise, whose number never ends and whose duration never terminates.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 5:

﴿As your Lord brought you forth from your house in truth﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), its estimated sense being: this condition of theirs in disliking it is like the condition of your bringing forth for war while they disliked it, and it is the dislike of what you saw of the distribution of spoils to the warriors. Or it is an attribute (sifah) of the verbal noun (masdar) of the verb estimated in His saying: ﴿to God and the Messenger﴾, meaning: the spoils were established for God and the Messenger ﷺ despite their dislike, an establishment like the establishment of your being brought forth by your Lord from your house, meaning Madinah, because it is his place of emigration (muhajar) and his dwelling, or his house therein, despite their dislike. ﴿And indeed a party of the believers were averse﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), i.e. He brought you forth while they were in a state of aversion. And this is because "the caravan of Quraysh came from Syria, and in it was great merchandise, and with it were forty riders, among them Abu Sufyan, 'Amr ibn al-'As, Makhramah ibn Nawfal and 'Amr ibn Hisham. Jibril, upon him be peace, informed the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he informed the Muslims, and they were pleased to meet it because of the abundance of wealth and the scarcity of men. When they set out, the news reached the people of Makkah, and Abu Jahl called out atop the Ka'bah: 'O people of Makkah, rescue! Rescue! For every swift and slow mount! Your caravan, your wealth: if Muhammad seizes it, you will never prosper after it, ever.' Three days before that, 'Atikah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib had seen that an angel descended from heaven, took a rock from the mountain, then flew off with it, and no house in Makkah remained without being struck by something of it. She related this to al-Abbas, and it reached Abu Jahl, who said: 'Are their men not content to prophesy until their women prophesy?' Abu Jahl set out with all the people of Makkah and went with them to Badr, a water-source where the Arabs used to gather for their market one day in the year. The Messenger of God ﷺ was at Wadi Dhafiran, and Jibril, upon him be peace, descended upon him with the promise of one of the two groups, either the caravan or Quraysh. He consulted his companions about it. Some of them said: 'Why did you not mention fighting to us, so that we might prepare for it? We only set out for the caravan.' He repeated it to them and said: 'The caravan has passed along the seashore, and this is Abu Jahl, who has come.' They said: 'O Messenger of God, go for the caravan and leave the enemy.' The Messenger of God ﷺ became angry. Then Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, stood and spoke, and they did well. Then Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah stood and said: 'Look to your affair and proceed in it, for by God, if you were to travel to 'Adan Abyan, not a man of the Ansar would stay behind you.' Then Miqdad ibn 'Amr said: 'Proceed as God has commanded you, for I am with you wherever you wish. We will not say to you what the Children of Israel said to Musa: "Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting here" (Qur'an 5:24). Rather, go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are fighting with you both.' The Messenger of God ﷺ smiled, then said: 'Advise me, O people,' and he meant the Ansar, because they were the majority of them, and they had stipulated, when they pledged allegiance to him at al-'Aqabah, that they were free of his obligation until he reached their dwellings. He feared that they would not see their support owed except against an enemy who attacked him in Madinah. Then Sa'd ibn Mu'adh stood and said: 'It is as if you mean us, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'Indeed.' He said: 'We have believed in you, confirmed you, and testified that what you have brought is the truth, and we have given you on that our covenants and pacts of hearing and obedience. So proceed, O Messenger of God, for what you intend. By Him who sent you with the truth, if you were to lead us into this sea and plunge into it, we would plunge in with you, not one man of us would stay behind, and we do not dislike that you meet our enemy with us. Indeed we are steadfast in war and truthful at the encounter, and perhaps God will show you from us what will delight your eye. So march with us in God's blessing.' His words invigorated him. Then he said: 'Proceed in God's blessing and rejoice, for God has promised me one of the two groups. By God, it is as if I am looking at the places where the people will fall.'"

And it is said that when he, upon him be prayers and peace, finished with Badr, it was said to him: "Go after the caravan." Al-'Abbas called out to him while he was in his bonds: "It is not fitting." He said to him: "Why?" He said: "Because God promised you one of the two groups, and He has given you what He promised you." Some of them disliked his saying this.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 6:

﴿They argue with you concerning the truth﴾ regarding your preference for jihad by making the truth manifest, in contrast to their preference for intercepting the caravan. ﴿After it had become clear﴾ to them that they would be given victory wherever they turned, by the informing of the Messenger, may blessings and peace be upon him. ﴿As if they were being driven to death while they looked on﴾ — i.e., they disliked fighting with the aversion of one who is driven to death while witnessing its causes. That was due to the smallness of their number and their lack of preparation, for it is related that they were on foot and there were only two riders among them. In this there is an indication that their argument was only due to the extreme of their fear and terror.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 7–8:

﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾. This is on the supposition of an implied "remember" (udhkur). "Iḥdā" is the second object of "yaʿiduukum," and "annahā" (that it) is substituted for it as a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). ﴿And you wished that the one not armed would be yours﴾, meaning the caravan, for there were only forty horsemen in it. For this reason they desired it and disliked meeting the enemy force, because of their numbers and equipment. "Al-shawka" (armed strength, sharpness) is a metaphor drawn from "wāḥidat al-shawk" (a single thorn). ﴿And Allah wills to establish the truth﴾, that is, to confirm it and make it prevail. ﴿By His words﴾, the revelation sent down in this situation, or by His commands to the angels to provide reinforcement. It is also read "bi-kalimatihi" (by His word). ﴿And to cut off the last of the disbelievers﴾, that is, to uproot them entirely. The meaning is: you want to obtain wealth and not encounter what you dislike, while Allah wills the exaltation of the religion and the manifestation of the truth, and what you gain is success in both abodes.

﴿That He might establish the truth and nullify falsehood﴾. That is, He did what He did, and this is not a repetition, because the first serves to explain the intended purpose and the difference between it and their purpose, and the second serves to explain the motive for leading the Messenger to choose the armed group and to give him victory over it. ﴿Even though the criminals dislike it﴾, that.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 9–10:

﴿When you sought help from your Lord⦆ is a substitution (badal) for (idh ya'idukum, "when He promised you"), or it is connected to His saying ﴿so that He might establish the truth⦆, or it is by supposing an implied "remember" (udhkur). Their seeking help was that, when they knew there was no escape (mahis) from fighting, they began to say: "O Lord, give us victory over Your enemy, aid us, O Helper of those who seek help." And it is related from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that "he (peace be upon him) looked at the polytheists, who were a thousand, and at his companions, who were three hundred. So he faced the qiblah and stretched out his hands, supplicating: 'O Allah, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O Allah, if this band perishes, You will not be worshipped on the earth.' He continued thus until his cloak (ridaʾ) fell from his shoulders, and Abu Bakr said: 'O Prophet of Allah, your urging of your Lord is enough, for He will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you.'"

﴿So He answered you: "Indeed I will reinforce you⦆ with (bi-anni mumiddukum), so he omitted the preposition and let the verb govern it directly. Abu ʿAmr read it with a kasra (innI), either intending the sense of saying, or treating istajaba (answered) as if it were qala (said), because answering is a form of speech. ﴿with a thousand of the angels, following one another⦆ — mut'biʿin, meaning following the believers, or following one another, from ardaftuhu (I followed him when I came after him); or following the believers as one another, or themselves being made to follow, from ardaftuhu iyyahu so that he followed him. Nafiʿ and Yaʿqub read mut-dafin with a fatha on the dal, meaning following, or mut-tabiʿin, in the sense that they were the vanguard of the army or its rearguard. It has also been read murdifin with a kasra and a damma on the ra', and its origin is murtadifayn, meaning mutaradifayn (in succession), then the ta' was assimilated into the dal, so two unvowelled consonants met, and the ra' was given a kasra according to the original form, or a damma by way of assimilation. It has also been read bi-alfin (with thousands), to agree with what is in Surat Al ʿImran. The way to reconcile this with the well-known reading is that what is meant by the thousand are those who were in the vanguard or the rearguard, or their notables and chiefs, or those among them who fought; and there is disagreement about whether they fought, though reports have been transmitted that indicate it.

﴿And Allah did not make it⦆, i.e., the reinforcement, ﴿except as good news⦆, except as a glad tidings to you of victory. ﴿and so that your hearts might be reassured thereby⦆, so that what was in them of trepidation (wajal) because of your small number and weakness would depart. ﴿And victory is only from Allah. Indeed Allah is Mighty, Wise⦆ — the reinforcement of the angels, the abundance of numbers, the equipment and the like, are intermediaries (wasa'it) which have no effect of their own; so do not reckon victory to come from them, nor despair of it through their absence.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 11:

﴿When He covered you with drowsiness﴾ is a second substitute (badal) for ﴿when He promised you﴾, to show a third blessing; or it is connected to "victory" (al-nasr), or to what is in ﴿with Allah﴾ of the sense of a verb, or to "He made" (ja'ala), or to an implied "remember" (udhkur). Nafi' read it with light stress (takhfif), from aghshaytuhu al-shay' (I covered him with the thing) when you cover him with it; and the subject in both readings is Allah, exalted is He. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿yaghshakum al-nu'as﴾ (drowsiness covers you) with the nominative. ﴿A security from Him﴾: security from Allah. It is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) in terms of meaning, since His saying ﴿He covers you with drowsiness﴾ implicitly carries the meaning of "you slumber" (tana'asun), and "yaghshakum" has that same meaning; and the word ﴿amanah﴾ is a verb for its doer. It is also permissible to intend by it faith (al-iman), in which case it is a verb of the one covered. And if one reads the last reading, one may take it as the verb of the drowsiness, metaphorically, because it belongs to his companions; or because it was necessary for him that it not cover them due to the intensity of fear, so when it did cover them, it is as if a security from Allah was obtained for him which, without it, would not have covered them, like his saying:

"Sleep fears to cover eyes... they fear you, so it is a shying, fleeing fugitive."

It was also read as ﴿amnatan﴾ on the pattern of ﴿rahmah﴾, and this is a dialect. ﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you thereby﴾ from the minor and major ritual impurity (hadath and janabah).

﴿And to remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾: meaning janabah, because it is from his imagining, or his whispering and his frightening them of thirst.

It is narrated that they alighted in a soft sand-dune where feet sink, without water, and they slept, and most of them had wet dreams, while the polytheists had overcome them at the water. So Satan whispered to them and said: "How will you be helped, when you have been overcome at the water, while you pray in a state of minor and major impurity, and you claim that you are the friends of Allah, and His Messenger is among you?" So they feared, and Allah sent down rain, and they were rained upon at night until the valley flowed, and they made cisterns on its bank, watered the mounts, bathed and performed ablution. The sand between them and the enemy became firm, so that feet stood firm on it, and the whispering departed.

﴿And that He may bind upon your hearts﴾ by trust in Allah's kindness towards them. ﴿And make firm thereby the feet﴾: that is, by the rain, so that they do not sink into the sand; or by the binding upon the hearts, so that they stand firm in the battle.

﴿When your Lord inspired﴾ is a third badal (substitution, an apposition) or is connected to يُثَبِّتَ (yuthabbit, "He may make firm"). ﴿to the angels: "I am with you"﴾ means in aiding and strengthening them, and it is the object of يُوحِي (yūḥī, "inspires"). It was also read with a kasra on the hamza, أنِّي (innī), on the basis that the verb implies speech, or that inspiration is treated as speech. ﴿So make firm those who believe﴾ by giving good news, or by increasing their numbers, or by fighting their enemies. In that case, his words ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾ serve as an explanation of ﴿I am with you, so make firm﴾. This indicates that they fought. Whoever prevents this interpretation makes the address in it to the believers, either by a change of address or on the ground that his words ﴿I will cast﴾ up to ﴿every fingertip﴾ are a dictation to the angels of what they should use to strengthen the believers, as if he had said: "Tell them my words." ﴿So strike above the necks﴾, meaning the upper parts of them, which are the places of slaughter, or the heads. ﴿And strike from them every fingertip﴾, meaning the fingers; that is, cut off their necks and sever their extremities.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 8, verses 13–14:**

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the striking (of the necks) or to the command to do it, and the address is to the Messenger, or to every one of those addressed before it. ﴿Because they (p-53) opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾ on account of their opposition to them both. The word (*shiqaq*, opposition) is derived from (*shaqq*, a split), because each of two adversaries is in a split opposite to the other's split, like (*mu'adah*, enmity) from (*'udwah*, enemy-side) and (*mukhasamah*, contention) from (*khasm*, opponent), which is the side. ﴿And whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, then indeed Allah is severe in punishment﴾ is a confirmation of the causal reasoning, or a warning of what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter after what befell them in this world.

﴿That is for you﴾: the address here is to the disbelievers by way of (*al-iltifat*, a shift from third person to second person address), and its position in the grammar is in the nominative, meaning: the matter is that, or, that is what befalls you. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 15–16:

﴿O you who believe, when you encounter those who disbelieve in a marching host﴾, a large number, such that because of their multitude they appear to be creeping forward. *Zahf* is the verbal noun of *zahafa al-sabiyyu*, when a child crawls on his buttocks little by little. It was used as a name for the host, its plural is *zuhuf*, and its position is accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). ﴿then do not turn your backs to them﴾ by fleeing, let alone when they are equal to you or fewer than you. It is most apparent that this verse is *muhkamah* (unabrogated, firm in its ruling) but specified (*makhsus*) by His saying: ﴿Urge the believers to fight﴾, and so on. It is permissible for *zahfan* to be an accusative of circumstance (*hal*) from the subject and the object, meaning: when you meet them while advancing toward one another, they creeping toward you and you creeping toward them, then do not flee. Or it may be a circumstance from the subject alone, and it would then be an indication of what would happen from them on the day of Hunayn, when they turned away, and they were twelve thousand.

﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾ intends a feigned retreat followed by a counter-attack (*karr ba'd al-farr*) and the deceiving of the enemy, for that is among the stratagems of war, ﴿except one who withdraws to fight﴾.

﴿or one who joins a company﴾, or one who retreats to join another company of the Muslims nearby in order to seek their help. Some scholars did not take nearness as a condition, based on what Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them) narrated: that he was in a *sariyyah* (a small military detachment) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent out, and they fled to Medina. I said: "O Messenger of Allah, we are the fleers (*farrarun*)!" He said: "Rather, you are the returners (*al-'akkarun*), and I am your company (*fi'ah*)."

The accusative of *mutaharrifan* and *mutahayyizan* is as a circumstance (*hal*). Otherwise it would be superfluous, having no governing effect. Alternatively, it is an exception from the ones who turn their backs, meaning: except a man who withdraws or joins a company. The morphological pattern of *mutahayyiz* is *mutafay'il*, not *mutafa''il*, for otherwise it would be *mutahawwiz*, since it derives from *haza yahuzu* (to possess, to gather to oneself).

﴿Then he has earned wrath from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾. This applies when the enemy does not exceed double (your number), based on His saying: ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you﴾, and so on. It has also been said that the verse is specified for the people of His household and those present with him in the battle.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 17–18:

﴿So you did not kill them﴾ by your own strength. ﴿But it was God who killed them﴾ by your victory, by giving you power over them, and by casting terror into their hearts.

It is narrated: "When Quraysh emerged from al-'Aqanqal, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'These are Quraysh, who have come with their arrogance and their pride, denying Your Messenger. O God, I ask You for what You have promised me.' Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and said: 'Take a handful of dust and throw it at them.' When the two hosts met, he took a handful of pebbles, threw it into their faces, and said, 'May their faces be disfigured.' No polytheist remained who was not distracted by his eyes, and they fled. The believers pursued them, killing and taking them captive. Then, when they returned, they turned to boasting, and a man would say, 'I killed and I took captives.' So this was revealed." The fa' (ف) is the answer to a conditional particle that is omitted, and its implied sense is: "If you boast of killing them, then you did not kill them, but God killed them." ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾, O Muhammad, a throw that would reach their eyes, and you were not capable of it. ﴿When you threw﴾ means when you performed the form of throwing. ﴿But God threw﴾ means He brought about the true completion of throwing, so it reached their eyes, all of them, until they fled and you were able to cut off their last remnant. You know that a term may be applied to the thing itself and also to its perfection and purpose. It was also said that the meaning is: you did not throw terror when you threw pebbles, but God threw terror into their hearts. It was also said that it was revealed concerning a spear-thrust with which Ubayy ibn Khalaf was struck on the Day of Uhud, from which no blood came out, so he began to bellow until he died; or concerning an arrow that was shot at the fortress on the Day of Khaybar, which struck Kinanah ibn Abi al-Huqayq on his bed. The majority hold the first view. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (وَلَكِنْ) with the light form (تخفيف), and the word following it in both places in the nominative.

﴿And that He might test the believers with a good trial from Him﴾, and that He might bestow upon them a great blessing through victory, spoils, and witnessing the signs; He did what He did. ﴿Indeed God is All-Hearing﴾ of their pleas and supplications. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of their intentions and their circumstances.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the good trial, or to the killing, or to the throwing. Its place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) is the nominative, meaning: the aim is that, or the matter is that. Its statement, ﴿and that God weakens the plot of the disbelievers﴾, is coordinated with it, meaning: the aim is the trial of the believers, the weakening of the plot of the disbelievers, and the nullifying of their stratagems.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read ﴿مُوهِنُ﴾ with the doubled letter (تشديد), and Hafs reads ﴿مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ﴾ with the genitive construction (إضافة) and the light form (تخفيف).

O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger (by obedience), when he calls you (﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اسْتَجِيبُوا لِلَّهِ ولِلرَّسُولِ﴾ "O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger" ... ﴿إذا دَعاكُمْ﴾ "when he calls you"). The pronoun in "he calls you" is singular, either because it refers back to what has preceded (Allah or the Messenger), or because the call of Allah is heard through the Messenger.

It is related that he (ﷺ) passed by Ubayy while he was praying, and he called him, but Ubayy hastened in his prayer. Then he came and said: "What prevented you from answering me?" He said: "I was praying." He said: "Were you not told in what was revealed to me: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger﴾?"

There is a difference of opinion regarding this. It is said that this is because answering him does not break the prayer, since the prayer is also a response. It is also said that his call was for a matter that does not admit delay, and the one praying may break the prayer for the sake of such a matter. The apparent meaning of the hadith fits the first view.

﴿لِما يُحْيِيكُمْ﴾ "that which gives you life" refers to the religious sciences, for they are the life of the heart, and ignorance is its death. It has been said:

*Do not be impressed by the finery of the ignorant man, for he is dead, and his garment is a shroud.*

Or it refers to that which brings you everlasting life in lasting bliss, from beliefs and deeds; or to jihad, for it is the cause of your survival, since if they abandoned it the enemy would overcome them and kill them; or to martyrdom, in accordance with His words: ﴿Nay, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for﴾.

﴿واعْلَمُوا أنَّ اللَّهَ يَحُولُ بَيْنَ المَرْءِ وقَلْبِهِ﴾ "And know that Allah comes between a man and his heart" is a figure of speech for the extent of His nearness to the servant, like His words: ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾. It is also a warning that He is aware of what is hidden in hearts, of what its owner may be heedless of; or an exhortation to hasten to sincerity of hearts and purifying them before Allah comes between a person and his heart by death or otherwise; or a depiction and imagery of His dominion over the servant's heart, so that He cancels his resolutions and changes his aims, and comes between him and disbelief if He wills his felicity, and between him and faith if He has decreed his wretchedness.

It is also read (بَيْنَ المَرِّ) with doubling (of the ra), by dropping the hamza, transferring its vowel onto the ra, and treating the pause and continuation according to the dialect of those who double it there.

﴿وَأنَّهُ إلَيْهِ تُحْشَرُونَ﴾ "and that to Him you will be gathered," so He will recompense you for your deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 25:

﴿And guard against a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong.﴾ Guard against a sin whose effect will encompass you: the spread of evil among you, complacency in enjoining what is good, division of the word, the emergence of innovations (bid'ah), and slackness in jihad.

As for His saying, لا تصيبن (*la tuṣībanna*, "will not strike"), it may be the response to the command (*jawāb al-amr*), meaning: your being struck does not strike only the wrongdoers among you, but encompasses you all. In this there is the point that the response to a conditional is uncertain, so the emphatic *nūn* (*nūn al-tawkīd*) does not suit it. However, since it contains the meaning of a prohibition, it is permissible, as in His saying: ﴿Enter your dwellings, lest they crush you﴾.

Or it is an attribute of فِتْنَةً (*fitnah*, "trial"), or it is for negation. In the latter case there is an irregularity, because the *nūn* does not enter a negated verb except in an oath.

Or it is a prohibition with the sense of "saying" implied, like his words:

*Until, when darkness fell and mingled, they came with watered milk. Have you ever seen a wolf?*

Or it is the response of an elided oath, like the reading of one who read لَتُصِيبَنَّ (*la-tuṣībanna*, with the *lām* of oath), though the two differ in meaning.

It may also be a prohibition following the command to guard against sin, forbidding exposure to wrongdoing, since its harm strikes the wrongdoer alone and returns upon him.

The *min* in مِنكم (*minkum*, "of you") is partitive (*tab'īḍ*) on the first readings, and explanatory (*tabyīn*) on the last two. Its benefit is to alert that wrongdoing from you is uglier than from others.

﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ (p-56)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 26:

﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land﴾: the land of Makkah, where the Quraysh oppressed you. The address is to the Muhajirun (the emigrants).

It is also said that the address is to the Arabs in general, for they were humbled under the rule of Persia and Byzantium. ﴿You feared that the people would snatch you away﴾: the disbelievers of Quraysh, or others besides them, for they were all hostile to them and opposed them. ﴿So He sheltered you﴾: by bringing you to Madinah, or by providing you with a refuge in which you could fortify yourselves against your enemies. ﴿And strengthened you with His help﴾: against the disbelievers, or through the support of the Ansar (the helpers), or through the reinforcement of the angels on the day of Badr. ﴿And provided you with good things﴾: from the spoils of war. ﴿So that you might be thankful﴾: for these blessings.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 27–28:

﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger﴾ by neglecting the obligations (fara'id) and the recommended practices (sunan), or by concealing the opposite of what you display, or by embezzlement from the spoils (ghulul fi al-maghanim).

It is narrated: "(He, upon whom be prayers and peace, besieged the Banu Qurayza for twenty-one nights. They asked him for reconciliation as he had made reconciliation with their brethren, the Banu al-Nadir, on condition that they would depart to their brethren at Adhri'at and Ariha in the land of Syria. He refused except that they should submit to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. They refused and said: Send to us Abu Lubaba, who was their advisor, because his dependents and his property were in their hands. So he sent him to them. They said: What do you think, should we submit to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh? He pointed to his throat, indicating that it meant slaughter. Abu Lubaba said: My feet had not moved until I knew that I had betrayed Allah and His Messenger, and then this was revealed. He bound himself to a pillar in the mosque and said: By Allah, I will not taste food or drink until I die or Allah accepts my repentance. He remained for seven days until he fell unconscious. Then Allah accepted his repentance. It was said to him: Your repentance has been accepted, so release yourself. He said: No, by Allah, I will not release myself until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the one who releases me. So he came to him and released him with his own hand. He said: Part of the completion of my repentance is that I abandon the house of my people in which I committed the sin, and that I divest myself of my wealth. He, upon whom be prayers and peace, said: A third will suffice for you, that you give it in charity.)"

The root of khawn is deficiency, just as the root of wafa' is completeness; its use for the opposite of trust (amanah) is because it implies that. ﴿and do not betray your trusts﴾ among yourselves, and it is either jazm by coordination with the first, or nasb as an answer introduced by the waw. ﴿while you know﴾ that you are betraying, or while you are scholars who distinguish the good from the bad.

﴿And know that your wealth and your children are a trial﴾ because they are the cause of falling into sin or punishment, or a test from Allah the Exalted by which He tries you through them, so their love should not drive you to betrayal as it did Abu Lubaba. ﴿And that with Allah is a great reward﴾ for whoever prefers the good pleasure of Allah over them and observes His limits concerning them. So direct your aspirations toward that which leads you to it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 27–28:

﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger﴾ by neglecting the obligations (fara'id) and the recommended practices (sunan), or by concealing the opposite of what you display, or by embezzlement from the spoils (ghulul fi al-maghanim).

It is narrated: "(He, upon whom be prayers and peace, besieged the Banu Qurayza for twenty-one nights. They asked him for reconciliation as he had made reconciliation with their brethren, the Banu al-Nadir, on condition that they would depart to their brethren at Adhri'at and Ariha in the land of Syria. He refused except that they should submit to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. They refused and said: Send to us Abu Lubaba, who was their advisor, because his dependents and his property were in their hands. So he sent him to them. They said: What do you think, should we submit to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh? He pointed to his throat, indicating that it meant slaughter. Abu Lubaba said: My feet had not moved until I knew that I had betrayed Allah and His Messenger, and then this was revealed. He bound himself to a pillar in the mosque and said: By Allah, I will not taste food or drink until I die or Allah accepts my repentance. He remained for seven days until he fell unconscious. Then Allah accepted his repentance. It was said to him: Your repentance has been accepted, so release yourself. He said: No, by Allah, I will not release myself until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the one who releases me. So he came to him and released him with his own hand. He said: Part of the completion of my repentance is that I abandon the house of my people in which I committed the sin, and that I divest myself of my wealth. He, upon whom be prayers and peace, said: A third will suffice for you, that you give it in charity.)"

﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan)﴾: guidance in your hearts by which you distinguish between truth and falsehood; or victory that distinguishes between the one who is right (al-muhiqq) and the one who is wrong (al-mubtil), through the exaltation of the believers and the humiliation of the disbelievers; or a way out of doubts; or deliverance from what you fear in both abodes; or a manifestation that makes your affair known and spreads your renown, from their saying "batta af'alu kadha" (I will certainly do such-and-such), until the furqan (dawn) shone forth, i.e., the morning. ﴿And He will expiate from you your misdeeds﴾: He will cover them. ﴿And forgive you﴾: by overlooking and pardoning you. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 30:

﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ is a reminder of what the Quraysh plotted against him (ﷺ) while he was in Makkah, so that he would be grateful for the blessing of God in his deliverance from their scheming and their overpowering of him. The meaning is: remember when they plot against you.

﴿To confine you﴾ in bonds or in prison, or to wound you severely, from the expression "he struck him until he made him (athbatahu) motionless, with no movement and no escape." It is also read (liyuthabbitūka) with the doubled letter, (liyubayyitūka) from al-bayt (overnight attack), and (liyuqayyidūka) meaning "to shackle you."

﴿Or kill you﴾ with their swords.

﴿Or expel you﴾ from Makkah. This is because, when they heard of the conversion of the Helpers (al-Anṣār) and their pledge of allegiance, they became apprehensive and gathered in the Council House (Dār al-Nadwa) to consult about his affair. Iblis entered upon them in the form of an old man and said: "I am from Najd. I heard of your gathering, so I wished to attend, and you will not lack from me an opinion and counsel." Abu al-Bukhturi said: "My opinion is that you imprison him in a room, seal its exits except for a small opening through which you pass him his food and drink, until he dies." The old man said: "Evil is this opinion. His people will come to you, fight you, and rescue him from your hands." Hisham ibn ʿAmr said: "My opinion is that you load him on a camel and expel him from your land, so he will not harm you by what he has done." He said: "Evil is this opinion. He will corrupt another people than yours and fight you with them." Abu Jahl said: "I see that you should take from every clan a young man, give him a sharp sword, and have them strike him one blow, so his blood will be scattered among the tribes, and the Banu Hashim will not be able to fight all of Quraysh. Then, if they demand the blood-money, we will pay it." He said: "This young man has spoken truly," and they dispersed according to his opinion. Then Gabriel came to the Prophet, peace be upon them both, informed him of the news, and commanded him to emigrate (al-hijrah). So he (ﷺ) had ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, sleep in his bed, and went out with Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, to the cave.

﴿They plot, and God plots﴾ by returning their plot upon them, or by requiting them for it, or by dealing with the schemers by bringing them out to Badr and making the Muslims appear few in their eyes, until they attacked them and were slain.

﴿And God is the best of plotters﴾, since their plotting carries no weight beside His plotting. The attribution of such things, which is fitting by way of pairing, is not to be used absolutely at the outset, because it contains an implication of blame.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 31–32:

﴿When Our verses are recited to them, they say: "We have heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this."﴾ This is the saying of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. Its attribution to all of them is the attribution to the people of what their leader (ra'is) did, for he was their storyteller (qassahum); or it is the saying of those who conspired against him (peace be upon him). This is the utmost of their obstinacy and their excessive stubbornness, for if they were able to do that, what prevented them from wishing it, when He had challenged them and rebuked them for their incapacity for ten years, then fought them with the sword, yet they did not produce a single surah in opposition, despite their pride and their excessive refusal to be overcome, especially in the domain of eloquence (bayan)?

﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients.﴾ That is, the tales that the ancients wrote down.

﴿And when they said: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ This too is from the words of that speaker, more eloquent in denial.

It is narrated that when al-Nadr said, "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients," the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Woe to you! It is the speech of Allah," and he said that.

The meaning is: if this Qur'an is indeed the truth, sent down, then rain stones upon us as a punishment for (p-58) denying it, or bring us some other painful punishment. What is intended by this is mockery and the display of complete certainty and conviction that it is false. "The truth" (al-Haqq) was also read in the nominative, with "this" (huwa) being a subject that is not a separator (fasl) pronoun; the benefit of the definiteness here is to indicate that what is conditioned upon it is that it is the truth in the aspect the Prophet (ﷺ) claims, namely that it is sent down, not the truth absolutely, since they allowed that it might correspond to reality without being sent down, like the fables of the ancients.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 33–34:

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ This explains what was the cause of their being granted respite and of the delay in answering their supplication. The lam (ل) is for emphasizing the negation, and it indicates that their punishment would be a punishment of total annihilation (isti'sal), while the Prophet ﷺ is among them, which is outside of His custom and not consistent with His judgment. As for the meaning of their seeking forgiveness, it is either the seeking of forgiveness by those among them who were believers, or their saying "O Allah, we seek Your forgiveness" (ghufranaka), or it is a supposition, in the sense that if they had sought forgiveness they would not have been punished, like His saying: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers.﴾

﴿And what is it with them that Allah should not punish them?⦆ What do they have that would prevent their punishment, once that (condition) has ceased, and how could they not be punished? ﴿While they bar access to the Sacred Mosque﴾ and this is their state; and among their barring of it is their forcing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers to emigrate, and their besieging them in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. ﴿And they were not its guardians﴾ entitled to the authority over it while they were polytheists; and this is a rejection of what they used to say: "We are the custodians of the House and the Sanctuary, so we bar whom we wish and admit whom we wish." ﴿Its guardians are only the righteous﴾ from among the polytheists, who do not worship other than Him in it. It was also said that both pronouns refer to Allah. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that they have no authority over it. As if by saying "most" he is alerting that among them are those who know and yet are obstinate; or he meant by it all of them, just as paucity is sometimes meant to denote non-existence.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 35:

﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but⦆ i.e., their supplication, or what they call prayer, or what they place in the position of prayer. ﴿Whistling﴾ (mukaa'), i.e., whistling. It is a fa'aal form from makā yamkū, meaning he whistled. It was also read with a short vowel (muka), like buka'. ﴿And clapping﴾ (tasdiyah), i.e., clapping, which they do, derived from al-sadā (echo), or from al-sadd (to turn away), with one of the two doubled letters replaced by a yā'. It was also read ﴿ṣalātahum﴾ in the accusative, as the predicate placed first, and the context of the statement is to establish that they deserve punishment, or that they have no right to the Mosque, for prayer of this kind does not befit one whose prayer is this.

It is narrated that they used to circumambulate the House naked, men and women alike, interlacing their fingers, whistling through them and clapping.

It was also said: they used to do this when the Prophet ﷺ intended to pray, confusing him and claiming that they too were praying. ﴿So taste the punishment﴾, meaning killing and captivity on the day of Badr. It was also said it refers to the punishment of the Hereafter. The lam (in al-'adhab) may be for specificity (al-'ahd), and the referent is: ﴿Bring upon us a punishment﴾ (Q. 8:32). ﴿Because you used to disbelieve﴾, both in belief and in action.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 36:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to averted [people] from the way of Allah﴾. It was revealed concerning the food-givers on the day of Badr, who were twelve men of Quraysh, each of whom fed, every day, ten camels. Or it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan, who hired two thousand men from the Arabs for the day of Uhud, besides those whom he enlisted from the Arabs, and spent on them forty ounces. Or it was revealed concerning the people of the caravan: when Quraysh were struck at Badr, it was said to them, "Help with this wealth against the war on Muhammad; perhaps we may obtain our revenge through it," and they did so. By ﴿the way of Allah﴾ is meant His religion and following His Messenger. ﴿So they will spend it﴾ in full. The first [statement] is likely a report of their spending in that situation, which is the spending of Badr, and the second is a report of their spending in the future, which is the spending of Uhud. It is possible that both refer to one [event], on the basis that the context of the first is to explain the purpose of the spending and the context of the second is to explain its outcome, and that it had not yet occurred. ﴿Then it will become for them a regret﴾, meaning remorse and grief at its loss without intention; He made its very substance become regret, and that is the consequence of their spending, as an intensification. ﴿Then they will be overcome﴾ in the end, even though the war between them was a back-and-forth (sijal) before that. ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, that is, those among them who remained upon disbelief, when some of them accept Islam. ﴿To Hell they will be gathered﴾, meaning driven.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 37–38:**

﴿That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾: the disbelievers from the believers, or corruption from righteousness. The lam (the particle of purpose, "that") is connected to ﴿they will be gathered﴾, or to ﴿they will be overcome﴾, or to what the polytheists spent in hostility toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of what the Muslims spent in supporting him. The lam is also connected to His saying ﴿then it will be a regret for them﴾. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read (liyumayyiza) from al-tamyiz (distinguishing), which is more emphatic than al-mayz (separation). ﴿And make the wicked, piled one upon another, and heap them all together﴾: He gathers them, and joins some of them to others, until they pile upon one another because of the extreme crowding; or He adds to the disbeliever what he spent, so that his punishment is increased by the full measure of the hoarders. ﴿Then He will put them in Hell﴾, all of them. ﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the wicked, since it is taken to refer to the wicked group, or to the spenders. ﴿They are the losers﴾: the complete ones in loss, for they have lost their own selves and their wealth.

﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾: meaning Abu Sufyan and his companions, and the meaning is "Say on their account." ﴿If they desist﴾ from opposing the Messenger (ﷺ) by entering Islam. ﴿Their past will be forgiven them﴾ of their sins. It is also read with the ta' and the kaf, on the basis that He addresses them, and (yaghfir) in the active voice, with Allah the Exalted as the subject. ﴿But if they return﴾ to fighting him. ﴿Then the way of the former peoples has already passed﴾: those who banded together against the prophets, who were destroyed, as happened to the people of Badr; so let them expect the like of that.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 39–40:

﴿And fight them until there is no more fitna (disbelief/polytheism)﴾ meaning there is no longer any shirk (associating partners with God) among them. ﴿And [until] religion is entirely for God﴾ and the false religions vanish from them. ﴿But if they cease﴾ from disbelief. ﴿Then indeed, God is Seeing of what they do﴾ so He will reward them for their ceasing from it and their embracing Islam. It is narrated from Ya'qub that he read "ta'malun" (tā'marūn, with the letter tā') according to the meaning: "Indeed God is Seeing of what you do" of jihad, the call to Islam, and the bringing out [of people] from the darkness of disbelief to the light of faith; so He will reward you. Making His reward conditional on their ceasing indicates that just as it calls for the reward of those who themselves embrace faith, it also calls for the reward of those who fight them for the cause (tasabbub, indirect causation).

﴿And if they turn away﴾ and do not cease. ﴿Then know that God is your Mawla (Protector/Patron)﴾ your helper, so trust in Him and do not care about their enmity toward you. ﴿How excellent a Protector﴾ He does not let down whoever takes Him as protector. ﴿And how excellent a Helper﴾ He is not overcome whoever He helps.

(p-60) ﴿And know that whatever you acquire as booty﴾, that is, whatever you seize from the disbelievers by force. ﴿Of anything﴾, of whatever falls under the term "thing," even a thread. ﴿Then to Allah belongs one-fifth of it﴾. The phrase *fa-anna* begins with a *mubtada'* (inchoative subject), whose *khabar* (predicate) is omitted; the sense is: "then it is established that to Allah belongs one-fifth of it." It has been read as *fa-inna* with a kasra. The majority hold that the mention of Allah is for glorification, as in His words ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾. The intended meaning is the division of the fifth among the five groups mentioned after it, ﴿and to the Messenger, and to the near kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾. It is as if He said: "to Allah belongs one-fifth of it, to be spent on these who are particularly entitled to it." Its ruling remains in force after him, except that the Messenger's share, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, is spent on the same things he used to spend it on, namely the welfare of the Muslims, as the two Shaykhs (Abu Bakr and 'Umar) may Allah be pleased with them both did. It is said that it goes to the Imam. It is said that it goes to the four remaining categories. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said that his share and the share of the near kin lapsed with his death, and the whole fifth is spent on the remaining three categories. From Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, it is reported that the matter is left to the judgment of the Imam, who spends it on whatever he sees as most important. Abu al-'Aliyah adopted the apparent meaning of the verse and said that it is divided into six parts, and the share of Allah is spent on the Ka'bah (the Sacred House), because it is reported that he, peace be upon him, used to take a handful from it and set it aside for the Ka'bah, and then divide the rest into five.

It is said that the share of Allah goes to the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*). It is said that it is added to the share of the Messenger ﷺ. The near kin are the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, because it is reported that he, peace be upon him, divided the share of the near kin between the two of them. 'Uthman and Jubayr ibn Mut'im, may Allah be pleased with them both, said to him: "These are your kinsmen, the Banu Hashim. We do not deny their merit, because of your standing which Allah has given you from among them. But what about our brothers from the Banu al-Muttalib? You gave to them and deprived us, though we and they are in one and the same position." He, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed they have never parted from us in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) or in Islam," and he interlaced his fingers.

It is said that it is only the Banu Hashim. It is said that all of Quraysh are included, rich and poor alike. It is said that it is restricted to their poor, like the share of the wayfarer. It is said that the whole fifth belongs to them, and that by the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer are meant those among them, the conjunction being for specification. The verse was revealed at Badr. It is said that the fifth was instituted at the expedition of Banu Qaynuqa', one month and three days after Badr, in the middle of Shawwal, at the beginning of the twentieth month after the Hijrah.

﴿If you have believed in Allah﴾: this is linked to an omitted element indicated by ﴿and know﴾. That is: if you have believed in Allah, then know that He has assigned the fifth to these, so hand it over to them, and be content with the remaining four-fifths. For practical knowledge, when it is commanded, is not to be taken as mere theoretical knowledge, since the former is the actual aim, and the essential purpose is action.

﴿And what We sent down upon Our servant﴾, Muhammad ﷺ, of the signs, the angels, and the victory. It has been read as *'Ubud-ina* with two dammas, meaning the Messenger ﷺ and the believers. ﴿On the Day of the Criterion﴾, the day of Badr, for on it Allah distinguished between truth and falsehood. ﴿The day the two hosts met﴾, the Muslims and the disbelievers. ﴿And Allah is over all things capable﴾, so He is able to grant victory to the few over the many and to support them with angels.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 42:

﴿When you were on the nearer side of the valley﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the Day of the Criterion" (yawm al-furqan). Al-'Udwa, with the three vowel patterns (ḍamma, kasra, fatḥa), means the bank or edge of a valley, and it has been recited with each of them. The well-known readings are with ḍamma and kasra, and this is the recitation of Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub. ﴿And they were on the farther side﴾ al-quswa, meaning the far side from Medina. It is the feminine of al-aqsa, and its regular form would have been the conversion of the waw into ya' as in al-dunya and al-'ulya, to distinguish the noun from the adjective. It came in its original form, as in al-qawd, and it is more commonly used than al-qusya. ﴿And the caravan﴾ meaning the caravan (al-'ir) or its commanders. ﴿Lower than you﴾ in a place lower than your place, meaning the coast. It is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf), standing in the position of the predicate, and the clause is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the adverb preceding it. Its purpose is to indicate the strength of the enemy and their reliance on the caravan, their eagerness to fight in its defence, and the settling of their hearts so that they would not abandon their positions and would exert the utmost effort; and the weakness of the Muslims' position and the precariousness of their affair, and the improbability of their victory by ordinary custom. Likewise he mentioned (p-61) the positions of both groups: the nearer side was soft, where feet sink and one cannot walk without difficulty, and there was no water in it, unlike the farther side. Likewise is His saying: ﴿And even if you had made an appointment with one another, you would have differed about the appointment﴾, meaning: even if you and they had agreed upon fighting, then you had known your condition and theirs, you would have differed about the appointment, out of awe of them and despair of victory over them. This was so that they would be certain that the victory which befell them was nothing but a work of God, Exalted, breaking the ordinary custom, and so they would increase in faith and gratitude. ﴿But﴾ He brought you together in this state without an appointment. ﴿That God might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾, a matter truly deserving to be carried out, which is the victory of His friends and the subjugation of His enemies.

And His saying: ﴿that whoever would perish might perish by clear proof, and whoever would live might live by clear proof﴾ is a substitute for it, or is connected to His saying "accomplished" (maf'ulan). The meaning: that whoever dies, dies by a proof he witnessed, and whoever lives, lives by an argument he saw, so that there would be no argument or excuse for him. The Battle of Badr is among the manifest signs. Or: that the disbelief of whoever disbelieved and the faith of whoever believed would proceed from the clarity of a clear proof, using the metaphor of perishing and living for disbelief and Islam. What is meant by "whoever perished" and "whoever lived" is those approaching destruction and life, or those whose state is this in God's knowledge and decree.

It has been recited as "liyahlaka" with a fatḥa, and Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu Bakr and Ya'qub recited "man ḥayiya" with the idgham undone, in accordance with the future form. ﴿And indeed God is Hearing, Knowing﴾ of the disbelief of whoever disbelieved and His punishment of them, and the faith of whoever believed and His reward of them. Perhaps the combination of the two attributes is because both matters involve speech and belief.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 43–44:

﴿When Allah shows them to you in your dream as few.﴾ The phrase is governed by an implied "remember" (udhkur), or it is a second substitute (badal) for "the Day of the Criterion" (yawm al-furqan), or it is connected to ʿalim (all-knowing), meaning: He knows the interests, when He makes them few in your eyes in your vision. Its purpose is that you inform your companions of it, so that it serves as reassurance for them and encouragement against their enemy.

﴿And had He shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart﴾, meaning you would have become cowardly. ﴿And you would have disputed about the matter﴾, meaning the matter of fighting, and your opinions would have divided between standing firm and fleeing.

﴿But Allah saved [you]﴾, meaning He bestowed safety from failure and dispute. ﴿Indeed, He is All-Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾, meaning He knows what will be in them and what changes their states.

﴿And when He showed them to you, when you met, as few in your eyes, and He made you few in their eyes﴾. The two pronouns are the objects of "showed" (yurika), and ﴿few﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (hal) referring to the second. He made them few in the eyes of the Muslims to such an extent that Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, said to the one beside him, "Do you think they are seventy?" He replied, "I think they are a hundred." This was for their reassurance and to confirm the Messenger's vision (ﷺ).

﴿And He makes you few in their eyes﴾, to such an extent that Abu Jahl said, "Muhammad and his companions are camel-eaters." He made them few in the eyes of the disbelievers before the clash of battle, so that they would become bold against them and not prepare for them. Then He made them numerous so that they would see them as twice their number, so that the abundance would surprise them, confound them, and break their hearts. This is among the great signs of that encounter. For although the eye may sometimes see the many as few and the few as many, not in this manner and not to this degree; rather, this is conceived only by Allah preventing the eyes from seeing some while not others, with the conditions being equal.

﴿That Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾. He repeated it because the verb being explained by it differs, or because the intended "matter" there is the sufficiency in the manner described, whereas here it is the exaltation of Islam and its people and the humiliation of polytheism and its party. ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned.﴾

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 45–46:

(p-62) ﴿O you who believe, when you encounter a company (fi'ah)﴾ — i.e., when you fight a group. He did not describe it [as enemy] because the believers were only ever meeting the disbelievers, and "liqa'" (encounter) is a term that has come to be used predominantly for fighting. ﴿Then stand firm﴾ for their encounter. ﴿And remember Allah much﴾ in the situations of war, supplicating to Him, seeking strength through His remembrance, and awaiting His victory. ﴿So that you may prosper﴾ — that you may attain your aim of victory and reward. In this there is an admonition that the servant should not let anything preoccupy him from the remembrance of Allah, that he should turn to Him in times of hardship, devote himself wholeheartedly to Him, with a free mind, certain that His kindness never leaves him in any circumstance.

﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute﴾ over differences of opinion, as you did at Badr or Uhud. ﴿Lest you lose heart (tafshalu)﴾ — this is the answer to the prohibition.

It has been said that it is conjoined to it (wa-li-dhalika qari'a: "and for this reason it was read"): ﴿and your strength (rihukum) depart﴾ in the jussive mood. The "wind" (rih) is a metaphor for state power, insofar as its affairs proceed and take effect, resembling a wind in its blowing and its penetration. It has also been said that what is meant is the literal wind, for victory only comes by a wind that Allah sends. And in the hadith: "I was helped by the east wind (al-sabā), and 'Ad were destroyed by the west wind (al-dabūr)."

﴿And be patient; indeed Allah is with the patient﴾ — with protection and victory.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 47:

﴿And do not be like those who went forth from their homes﴾ meaning the people of Makkah when they went out from it to protect the caravan. ﴿Insolently﴾ out of pride and exultation. ﴿And to be seen by the people﴾ so that they would praise them for courage and generosity. This was because when they reached al-Juhfah, a messenger of Abu Sufyan came to them saying: "Return, for your caravan has been saved." Abu Jahl said: "No, by God, we will not return until we reach Badr, and drink wine there, have singing girls play for us, and feed those Arabs who are present with us." But they came to it, and instead they were made to drink the cup of death, and the mourning women wailed over them. So He forbade the believers from being like them, insolent and showing off, and commanded them to be people of God-consciousness and sincerity, since forbidding something is a command to its opposite. ﴿And they hinder from the way of God﴾ is coordinated with "insolently" if it is taken as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause, and likewise if it is taken as an object of purpose, but in the sense of a verbal noun. ﴿And God is encompassing of what they do﴾ so He will recompense you for it.

﴿And when Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾: this is governed by an implied verb, *idhkur* (اذْكُرْ, "remember"). ﴿Their deeds﴾ refers to their hostility towards the Messenger (ﷺ) and other things, as Satan whispered to them. ﴿And he said, "No one among mankind can overcome you today, and I am your protector"﴾: this is a statement from the soul (*maqalah nafsaniyyah*). The meaning is that he cast it into their hearts and gave them the illusion that they could not be defeated or resisted, because of their large numbers and equipment. He also led them to believe that following him in what they considered acts of devotion would make him their protector, until they said, "O Allah, give victory to the more rightly guided of the two parties and the better of the two religions." The phrase ﴿no one can overcome you﴾ has *lakum* as its *khabar* (predicate), or *sifatuhu* (its attribute). It is not its *silah* (the complement of a relative clause), otherwise it would be in the accusative, as in your saying: "No one is striking Zayd here."

﴿When the two hosts sighted each other﴾: that is, when the two groups met. ﴿He turned back on his heels﴾: he withdrew backwards, meaning that his scheme failed, and what he had given them the illusion of, that he was their protector, became the cause of their destruction. ﴿And he said, "I am innocent of you. Indeed I see what you do not see. Indeed I fear Allah"﴾: that is, he disassociated himself from them, feared for them, and despaired of their situation when he saw Allah reinforcing the Muslims with angels. It has also been said: when Quraysh gathered to march out, they recalled the enmity between them and the Banu Kinanah, which nearly deterred them. Iblis then appeared to them in the form of Suraqah ibn Malik al-Kinani and said, "No one can overcome you today, and I am your protector against the Banu Kinanah." When he saw the angels descending, he turned back. He had his hand in the hand of al-Harith ibn Hisham, who said to him, "Where are you going? Will you abandon us in this situation?" He replied, "Indeed I see what you do not see," and he pushed al-Harith in the chest and departed, and they were routed. When they reached Makkah, they said, "Suraqah has routed the people." This reached him, and he said, "By Allah, I did not know of your march until your defeat reached me." When they embraced Islam, they realised that it had been Satan.

On this view, the meaning of his words ﴿Indeed I fear Allah﴾ may be: "I fear that a harm from the angels will befall me, or that He will destroy me." The time would then be the appointed time, since at that moment he saw what he had not seen before. The first interpretation is what al-Hasan said, and Ibn Bahr preferred it. ﴿And Allah is severe in punishment﴾: this may be part of his speech, or it may be a new, independent sentence.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 49:

﴿When the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say﴾ and those who have not yet settled into faith and there remains in their hearts a doubt. It is said that they are the polytheists (mushrikun). It is also said that they are the hypocrites (munafiqun), and the conjunction (al-'atf) is because the two descriptions differ. ﴿Their religion has deluded these﴾, meaning the believers, ﴿so that they expose themselves to what they have no power to face; thus they went out, and they were three hundred and some ten, about a thousand.﴾ ﴿And whoever puts his trust in Allah﴾ is their answer. ﴿Indeed Allah is Mighty (ʿAziz)﴾, the Victorious who does not humiliate whoever seeks refuge in Him, even if he is few. ﴿Wise (Hakim)﴾, who does by His far-reaching wisdom what the intellect finds remote and is unable to comprehend.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 50–51:

﴿And if you could see﴾ — i.e., "and if you (O Muhammad) saw." Indeed, "law" (if only / if) makes the present tense past, the opposite of "in" (if). ﴿when the angels take those who disbelieve﴾ — at Badr. "Idh" (when) is an adverb governed by "tara" (you see), and its object is omitted: i.e., "and if you saw the disbelievers, or their state, at that time." The angels are the subject of "yatawaffa" (take). This is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Amir with the feminine ta' (tatawaffa). It is also permissible for the subject to be a pronoun referring to God, Mighty and Majestic, and then it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿they strike their faces﴾; the clause is in the state (hal) of "alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieve). The pronoun is used in place of the waw (conjunction), and in the first case it is a state of them or of the angels, or of both, because it contains both pronouns. ﴿and their backs﴾ — their faces, or their buttocks. It is likely that the intended meaning is generalization of the striking, i.e., they strike whatever is before them and whatever is behind them. ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾ — it is conjoined to "yadribuna" (they strike) with an implied "saying": i.e., and they say, "Taste," as a announcement of the punishment of the Hereafter to them. It was said: they had with them rods of iron, and whenever they struck, fire blazed from them. The answer to "law" is omitted, to cut short the matter and to magnify its terror.

﴿That﴾ — the striking and the punishment. ﴿is because of what your hands have sent forward﴾ — because of what they earned of disbelief and sins; and this is the predicate of "dhalika." ﴿And that Allah is not unjust to the servants﴾ — conjoined to "ma" (what), to indicate that its causality is restricted by its being combined with the other (i.e., God's justice): for were it not so, it would be possible for Him to punish them without their sins, not that He would not punish them for their sins. For abandoning punishment of one who deserves it is not injustice, either by law or by reason, such that the negation of injustice would serve as a cause for punishment. "Zallam" (intensive form) here denotes intensification, on account of "the servants" (i.e., the many servants).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 52–54:

﴿As the case of the people of Pharaoh﴾: that is, the case of these people is like the case of the people of Pharaoh, which is their practice and their way (ṭarīq) in which they persisted (dā'ū fīhi), meaning they continued in it. ﴿And those before them﴾: before the people of Pharaoh. ﴿Denied the signs of Allah﴾: an explanation of their case. ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾: just as He seized these people. ﴿Indeed Allah is Strong, Severe in punishment﴾: nothing can overcome Him in repelling it.

(p-64) ﴿That﴾: a reference to what befell them. ﴿Because Allah﴾: by reason of the fact that Allah. ﴿Would never change a favor He had bestowed upon a people﴾: changing it (mubaddilan iyyāhā) into a calamity (niqmah). ﴿Until they change what is in themselves﴾: they alter their state from a state into a worse one, like the change of Quraysh in their maintenance of kinship ties (ṣilat al-raḥim), and their restraint from harming the signs and the messengers by opposing the Messenger (ﷺ) and those of them who followed him, and their striving to shed their blood, and their denial of the signs and their mockery of them, and other things they introduced after the mission (al-mab'ath). The cause is not that Allah does not change the favor He bestowed upon them until they change their state; rather, what is understood from it is that His habit is to change it when they change their state. The original form of yakun was yakūnu; the vowel was dropped for the jussive, then the wāw was dropped due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, then the nūn was dropped for lightness, due to its resemblance to the soft letters.

﴿And that Allah is Hearing﴾ of what they say. ﴿Knowing﴾ of what they do.

﴿As the case of the people of Pharaoh and those before them, they denied the signs of their Lord, so We destroyed them for their sins and drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾: a repetition for emphasis, and for what is connected to it of indication of ingratitude for favors by His saying ﴿the signs of their Lord﴾, and an explanation of what the people of Pharaoh were seized with. It was said that the first is to liken the disbelief and the seizing to it, and the second is to liken the change in the favor because of their changing what is in themselves. Each of them refers to the denying groups, or to the drowned Copts and the slain of Quraysh. ﴿They were wrongdoers﴾: wronging themselves by disbelief and sins.

﴿As the case of the people of Pharaoh and those before them, they denied the signs of their Lord, so We destroyed them for their sins and drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾: a repetition for emphasis, and for what is connected to it of indication of ingratitude for favors by His saying ﴿the signs of their Lord﴾, and an explanation of what the people of Pharaoh were seized with. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verses 55–56:

﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve﴾: they persisted in disbelief and became firmly rooted in it. ﴿So they do not believe﴾: so no faith is to be expected from them. It may be that this is a report about a people who were sealed (maṭbūʿūn) upon disbelief, that they do not believe. The fa' (fa) here is for conjunction (ʿaṭf) and for drawing attention to the fact that the realisation of the thing conjoined (maʿṭūf ʿalayhi) necessitates the realisation of what is conjoined (maʿṭūf). His words: ﴿those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time﴾ are a substitute (badal) for ﴿those who disbelieve﴾, a substitute of part (badal al-baʿḍ) for clarification (lil-bayān) and specification (wa-l-takhṣīṣ). They are the Jews of Qurayẓa. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made a covenant with them that they would not aid against him, but they helped the polytheists with weapons and said: "We forgot." Then he made a covenant with them again, and they broke it and colluded with them against him on the day of the Trench (al-Khandaq). Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf also rode to Mecca and formed an alliance with them. The min (from) is to imply that the covenant carries the sense of taking (al-akhdh), and by "time" (marrah) is meant a time of covenanting or of warring.

﴿And they do not fear﴾: the disgrace of treachery and its consequence; or they do not fear Allah concerning it, or His giving victory to the believers and His empowering them over them.

﴿So if you encounter them﴾, that is, if you come upon them and gain the upper hand over them, ﴿in war, then scatter those behind them﴾, that is, disperse them from their opposition and deter others from it by killing them and inflicting harm on them, ﴿those behind them﴾, meaning the disbelievers who are behind them. This seems to be a metathesis of shadhara, and the meaning is the same, since when those behind them are scattered, the scattering has been carried out upon those in the rear. ﴿So that they may take heed﴾, that is, so that those who are scattered may be admonished.

﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾, that is, from those with whom you have a treaty, ﴿treachery﴾, meaning the breaking of a covenant, indicated by signs that become apparent to you, ﴿then throw back to them﴾, that is, cast their covenant back to them, ﴿on equal terms﴾, that is, with justice and a straightforward course regarding enmity, and do not engage them in battle, for that would be treachery on your part. (And let not those who disbelieve think that they have escaped.) This is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, and His words ﴿those who disbelieved have outstripped﴾ are its two objects. Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and Ḥafṣ read (yaḥsabanna) with the ya' (p-65), on the basis that the subject is a pronoun referring to someone, or ﴿those who are behind them﴾, or ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, and the first object is "themselves" (anfusahum), which is omitted due to its repetition. Or it is taken as an implied "that they outstripped" (an sabaqū), which is weak, because the verbal an (an al-maṣdariyyah) is like the relative pronoun and therefore is not omitted. Or the verb is applied to (annahum lā yuʿjizūn) with the fatḥah according to the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir, with an (anna) and lā being a redundant particle (ṣilah), and ﴿sabaqū﴾ being a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) meaning "outstripping," i.e., "escaping." The more apparent view is that it is a causal clause (taʿlīl) for the prohibition, meaning: do not think they have outstripped and escaped, because they cannot escape God, or they will not find that their pursuer is incapable of overtaking them. The same applies if you read inna with a kasrah, except that it is a causal clause by way of a new sentence (istiʾnāf). Perhaps the verse serves to remove what one is warned against: abandoning the covenant and alerting the enemy. It was also said that it was revealed concerning one who escaped from the rout of the polytheists.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 60–61:

﴿And prepare﴾ O believers, ﴿against them﴾ (i.e., against those who break the covenant, or against the unbelievers) ﴿whatever you can of strength﴾, meaning whatever by which one can strengthen oneself in war.

And on the authority of ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, who said: I heard him (ﷺ) say on the pulpit: "Indeed, strength is archery," and he said it three times. Perhaps he (ﷺ) singled it out for mention because it is the strongest of them. ﴿And of steeds kept ready﴾: this is a term for the horses that are tethered (rubiṭa) in the way of God. It is a form of fiʿāl in the sense of mafʿūl, or a verbal noun that has been used as a name. It is said: rabaṭa, rabṭan, wa-ribāṭan; and rābaṭa, murābaṭatan, wa-ribāṭan. Or it is the plural of rabīṭ, like faṣīl and fiṣāl. It has also been read as "rubuṭ al-khayl" with the ḍamma and the sukūn on the bāʾ, as the plural of ribāṭ, and its conjunction with "strength" is like the conjunction of Gabriel and Michael with "the angels." ﴿You strike terror with it﴾: you frighten with it. It is related from Yaʿqūb that he read "turhibūna" with the shadda, and the pronoun refers either to "whatever you can" or to the preparation.

﴿The enemy of God and your enemy﴾: meaning the unbelievers of Mecca. ﴿And others besides them﴾: others from among the unbelievers apart from them. It has been said they are the Jews; it has been said they are the hypocrites; it has been said they are the Persians. ﴿You do not know them﴾: you do not recognize them by their persons. ﴿God knows them﴾: He recognizes them. ﴿Whatever you spend on anything in the way of God will be repaid to you﴾: its reward. ﴿And you will not be wronged﴾: by the losing of the deed or the diminishing of the reward.

﴿And if they incline﴾: they lean, and from this comes "janāḥ" (wing). It may be transitive with lām and with ilā. ﴿To peace﴾: to reconciliation or to submission. Abū Bakr read it with a kasra. ﴿Then incline to it﴾: and make a covenant with them. The feminine pronoun is because peace is treated as the opposite of war in this regard. He said:

Peace: take from it what you are content with, and war: its breaths are enough for you as a mouthful.

It has also been read "fa-ujnuḥ" with a ḍamma. ﴿And put your trust in God﴾: and do not fear their concealed treachery, for God will protect you from their plotting and will turn it back upon them. ﴿Indeed He is the Hearing﴾ of their words, ﴿the Knowing﴾ of their intentions. The verse is specific to the People of the Book because it is connected to their story; it has been said that it is general, and that it was abrogated by the verse of the sword.
